claim_audit: 0:9600 Pareto's 1896 observation about Italian land concentration correctly cited; the pea-pod garden story is a popular but weakly documented anecdote. James's $600 + $400 + ~$600/month after-tax raise vs Sarah's $200 supports "over $1,000 more" before his higher restaurant spending and used-car operating costs. $1,000/month rent gap x 12 x 10 = $120,000 correct. "Housing, transportation and income represent ~80% of expenses" - housing plus transportation are roughly half of average household spending in BLS Consumer Expenditure data, so 80% is overstated (and income is not an expense).

0:9600 Buffett bet (2008-2017): S&P 500 index fund +125.8% versus five funds-of-funds +2.8% to +87.7% matches Buffett's 2017 shareholder letter; describing managers as constantly trying to time the market is a characterization.

9600:19110 40% vs 25% of $70,000 = $28,000 vs $17,500, difference $10,500 correct; $10,000/year at 8% for 30 years = ~$1.13M (stored "$1.2 $2 million" garbled ASR). $700 x 72 = $50,400 correct; $700/month at 8% for 20 years = ~$412K, but the payment lasts six years in the script's own setup - investing $700/month for six years then letting it grow to year 20 gives ~$189K, so "$400,000 decision" overstates. "Income has unlimited upside, expenses a floor" is a rhetorical simplification. "Wealthy people order expensive wine without checking the price" is an unsupported generalization.

topic.analysis: Big-wins personal finance: prioritize housing, transportation and income over micro-budgeting. Broad audience; evergreen and well-trodden (Ramit Sethi-style "big wins"), packaged with the Pareto label. Practical but repetitive.
topic.novelty_and_corpus_angle: Original angle: quantify each viewer's personal 80/20 with an on-screen audit of their top three expense lines versus 20 small categories, using one consistent opportunity-cost calculator.
